about: The scripted AI lesson for p5-momentum (2026-11-28, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p5-newtons-laws and p5-stopping-distance.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about momentum: why a moving lorry is so hard to stop, and what happens when things collide.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. A 2 kg trolley accelerates at 3 m/s². What is the resultant force on it?

wrong.divide: Not quite: multiply the mass by the acceleration: 2 × 3 = 6 N.
wrong.add: Not quite: multiply, do not add: 2 × 3 = 6 N.

steps.question: Second: which of these is a vector, with a size and a direction?
steps.right: Yes: velocity is speed in a given direction, so it is a vector.

wrong.speed: Not quite: speed has no direction, so it is a scalar. Velocity is speed in a given direction.
wrong.mass: Not quite: mass has no direction, so it is a scalar. Velocity has a direction.

idk.hint: A vector has a direction. Which of these says which way?

steps.answerWhy: Velocity is speed in a given direction, so it is a vector; speed and mass are scalars.

steps.text: Now this lesson. A slow, heavy lorry and a fast car can both be hard to stop. What they share is a quantity that combines mass and velocity.
Mass × velocity is called momentum.
The equation is p = m v. Here p is the momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m/s), m is the mass in kilograms (kg) and v is the velocity in m/s.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A 1500 kg car travels at 20 m/s. What is its momentum?
steps: Write the equation: p = m v.

steps.question: Your turn. A 60 kg runner moves at 5 m/s. What is the runner's momentum, in kg m/s?
steps.right: Yes: p = m v = 60 × 5 = 300 kg m/s.

wrong.other: Not quite: 300 kg m/s. p = m v = 60 × 5 = 300 kg m/s.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 300 kg m/s. Multiply the mass by the velocity: 60 × 5 = 300 kg m/s.
wrong.add: Not quite: 300 kg m/s. Multiply, do not add: 60 × 5 = 300 kg m/s.

steps.question: A 50 g ball moves at 20 m/s. What is its momentum, in kg m/s? (1000 g = 1 kg.)

wrong.other: Not quite: 1 kg m/s. 50 g = 0.05 kg, and p = 0.05 × 20 = 1 kg m/s.
wrong.grams: Not quite: 1 kg m/s. Change grams to kilograms first: 50 g = 0.05 kg. Then 0.05 × 20 = 1 kg m/s.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 1 kg m/s. Multiply the mass in kg by the velocity: 0.05 × 20 = 1 kg m/s.

idk.hint: Change 50 g into kilograms first: 1000 g = 1 kg.

steps.text: Velocity has a direction, so momentum does too. A quantity with a size and a direction is called a vector quantity.

Pick one direction as positive; momentum the other way is then negative. Two cars of the same mass driving towards each other at the same speed have momenta (the plural of momentum) of the same size, one positive and one negative.

steps.question: A 2 kg ball moves right at 3 m/s. A 1 kg ball moves left at 4 m/s. Taking right as positive, what is their total momentum, in kg m/s?
steps.right: Yes: 2 × 3 = +6 kg m/s and 1 × 4 = 4 kg m/s to the left, which is −4. Total: 6 − 4 = 2 kg m/s, to the right.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2 kg m/s. Right is +6 kg m/s and left is −4 kg m/s, so the total is 6 − 4 = 2 kg m/s.
wrong.add: Not quite: 2 kg m/s. The balls move in opposite directions, so one momentum is negative: 6 − 4 = 2 kg m/s.
wrong.sign: Not quite: 2 kg m/s. Right is positive, and the bigger momentum, 6 kg m/s, is to the right: 6 − 4 = +2 kg m/s.

idk.hint: Work out each momentum. The one moving left counts as negative.

steps.answerWhy: The right-moving ball has +6 kg m/s and the left-moving one −4 kg m/s, so the total is +2 kg m/s.

steps.question: A 1000 kg car moves at 10 m/s. How fast must a 500 kg car move to have the same momentum?

wrong.same: Not quite: with half the mass at the same speed, it has half the momentum. It needs twice the speed: 500 × 20 = 10 000 kg m/s.
wrong.half: Not quite: a smaller mass needs a bigger speed, not a smaller one. 500 × 20 = 10 000 kg m/s.

idk.hint: The first car has 1000 × 10 = 10 000 kg m/s. Divide that by 500 kg to find the speed.

steps.answerWhy: The first car has 10 000 kg m/s. The second needs v = 10 000 ÷ 500 = 20 m/s.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is momentum?
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: momentum is mass × velocity, p = m v, measured in kg m/s, and like velocity it has a direction.

steps.text: When objects collide or push apart, they push on each other, and their momenta change.
A group of objects with no outside forces acting on it is called a closed system.
In a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. This rule is called conservation of momentum.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a still 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. How fast do they move off?
steps: The total after is the same: 6 kg m/s.

steps.question: Your turn. A 4 kg trolley at 5 m/s hits a still 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. How fast do they move off, in m/s?
steps.right: Yes: momentum 4 × 5 = 20 kg m/s, shared by 5 kg: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s.

wrong.other: Not quite: 4 m/s. Momentum before is 4 × 5 = 20 kg m/s. After, 5 kg carries it: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s.
wrong.same: Not quite: 4 m/s. The same momentum is now carried by more mass, so they move more slowly: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s.
wrong.momentum: Not quite: 20 kg m/s is the momentum. Divide by the combined mass, 5 kg: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s.

idk.hint: Momentum before = 4 × 5. After, the trolleys move together with a mass of 5 kg.

steps.answerWhy: Momentum before is 4 × 5 = 20 kg m/s. After, the 5 kg pair has the same momentum, so v = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s.

steps.text: In physics, an explosion is any event where things that were still push apart. Before a cannon fires, nothing moves, so the total momentum is zero. After it fires, the ball goes forwards and the cannon rolls back.

steps.question: Why must the cannon roll backwards as the ball goes forwards?

options.text: The momenta must still add up to zero
The ball pushes air back onto it

steps.right: Yes: the ball's forward momentum is cancelled by the cannon's backward momentum, so the total stays zero.

wrong.other: Not quite: the momenta must still add up to zero.
wrong.air: Not quite: it would roll back even with no air. The total momentum was zero, so the cannon must move back to balance the ball.
wrong.lighter: Not quite: its mass hardly changes. The total momentum was zero, so the cannon must move back to balance the ball.

idk.hint: What was the total momentum before firing? It must be the same after.

steps.answerWhy: The total momentum was zero before, so after firing the ball's forward momentum must be balanced by the cannon moving back.

steps.question: A 0.02 kg bullet leaves a still 4 kg rifle at 400 m/s. How fast does the rifle move backwards (recoil), in m/s?
steps.right: Yes: the bullet has 0.02 × 400 = 8 kg m/s, so the rifle has 8 kg m/s backwards: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2 m/s. The bullet has 0.02 × 400 = 8 kg m/s, so the rifle has 8 kg m/s back: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s.
wrong.same: Not quite: 2 m/s. The rifle has the same momentum as the bullet, not the same speed. 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s.
wrong.momentum: Not quite: 8 kg m/s is the momentum. Divide by the rifle's mass: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s.

idk.hint: Find the bullet's momentum. The rifle has the same amount, backwards.

steps.answerWhy: The bullet has 0.02 × 400 = 8 kg m/s, so the 4 kg rifle has 8 kg m/s backwards: v = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s.

steps.text: Momentum is conserved even when something does not seem to move. A snowball hitting a wall passes its momentum to the wall and the Earth, which are so massive they barely move.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does conservation of momentum say?
points: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it.
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it.

steps.text: A resultant force on an object changes its velocity, so it changes its momentum. Momentum after minus momentum before is called the change in momentum, written m Δv (Δ means "change in").
Putting F = m a together with a = Δv ÷ Δt gives F = m Δv ÷ Δt.
In words: force = change in momentum ÷ time taken. F is in newtons (N), m Δv in kg m/s, and Δt, the time taken, in seconds (s).
Force equals the rate of change of momentum: how much the momentum changes each second. The same change in momentum spread over a longer time needs a smaller force.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A 0.5 kg ball at 10 m/s is caught and stopped in 0.1 s. What force stops it?
steps: Write the equation: F = m Δv ÷ Δt.

steps.question: Your turn. The same ball is caught with soft hands that stop it in 0.5 s. What force stops it now, in N?
steps.right: Yes: F = 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 N, much less than 50 N.

wrong.other: Not quite: 10 N. The change in momentum is still 5 kg m/s, so F = 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 N.
wrong.times: Not quite: 10 N. Divide the change in momentum by the time: 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 N.
wrong.same: Not quite: 10 N. The longer time means a smaller force: 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 N.

idk.hint: The change in momentum is still 5 kg m/s. Divide it by the new time, 0.5 s.

steps.answerWhy: The change in momentum is 5 kg m/s, so F = 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 N: a longer stop means a smaller force.

steps.question: Why does a crash mat in a gym help when someone lands on it?

options.text: The stop takes longer, so the force is smaller
It makes the momentum change zero

steps.right: Yes: the mat makes the stop take longer, so the momentum changes more slowly and the force is smaller.

wrong.other: Not quite: the stop takes longer, so the force is smaller.
wrong.zero: Not quite: the person still stops, so their momentum still changes by the same amount. The mat makes it take longer, so the force is smaller.
wrong.lighter: Not quite: the person's mass does not change. The mat makes the stop take longer, so the force is smaller.

idk.hint: The person stops either way. What does the soft mat change about the stop?

steps.answerWhy: The change in momentum is the same, but the mat makes the stop take longer, so the rate of change of momentum, and the force, is smaller.

steps.text: Many safety features work the same way. Airbags, seat belts, crumple zones, cycle helmets and soft playground surfaces all make a collision last longer, so the force on the person is smaller.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does force equal, in terms of momentum?
points: Force equals the change in momentum divided by the time taken.
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: force equals the change in momentum divided by the time taken, so a longer collision means a smaller force.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: what is the unit of momentum?

wrong.newton: Not quite: the newton is the unit of force. Momentum is mass × velocity, in kg m/s.
wrong.accel: Not quite: m/s² is the unit of acceleration. Momentum is in kg m/s.

idk.hint: Momentum = mass × velocity. Multiply their units.

steps.answerWhy: Momentum is mass (kg) × velocity (m/s), so its unit is kg m/s.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: a 3 kg ball moves at 4 m/s. What is its momentum?

wrong.divide: Not quite: multiply the mass by the velocity: 3 × 4 = 12 kg m/s.
wrong.add: Not quite: multiply, do not add: 3 × 4 = 12 kg m/s.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: two objects collide in a closed system. Which is true of their total momentum?

options.text: It is the same before and after

steps.right: Yes: in a closed system, momentum is conserved.

wrong.other: Not quite: it is the same before and after.
wrong.up: Not quite: in a closed system the total momentum does not change.
wrong.down: Not quite: in a closed system the total momentum does not change.

idk.hint: Conservation of momentum says the total momentum in a closed system does not change.

steps.answerWhy: In a closed system, the total momentum before equals the total after.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: two skaters stand still, then push each other apart. Which is true just after?

options.text: Their momenta are equal and opposite
The heavier one has more momentum

steps.right: Yes: they have equal momentum in opposite directions, so the total is still zero.

wrong.other: Not quite: their momenta are equal and opposite.
wrong.heavier: Not quite: the total must stay zero, so their momenta are equal in size. The heavier one moves more slowly.
wrong.none: Not quite: both move, so both have momentum. It is equal and opposite, so the total is zero.

idk.hint: The total momentum was zero before the push.

steps.answerWhy: The total momentum stays zero, so the skaters have momenta of equal size in opposite directions.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: which is equal to the resultant force on an object?
steps.right: Yes: force is the rate of change of momentum.

wrong.other: Not quite: change in momentum ÷ time.
wrong.times: Not quite: force is the change in momentum divided by the time.
wrong.mv: Not quite: mass and velocity are multiplied to give momentum. Force is the change in momentum divided by the time.

idk.hint: Force is the rate of change of momentum.

steps.answerWhy: F = m Δv ÷ Δt: force equals the change in momentum divided by the time taken.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: how do airbags reduce injuries in a crash?

options.text: The stop takes longer, so the force is smaller
They make the person stop more quickly
They take away the person's momentum

steps.right: Yes: a longer stop means a smaller rate of change of momentum, so a smaller force.

wrong.other: Not quite: the stop takes longer, so the force is smaller.
wrong.quicker: Not quite: a quicker stop would mean a bigger force. Airbags make the stop take longer.
wrong.remove: Not quite: the person still stops, so their momentum still changes by the same amount. Airbags make it change more slowly.

idk.hint: The person stops either way. What does the airbag change?

steps.answerWhy: The airbag makes the stop take longer, so the momentum changes more slowly and the force is smaller.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.
